headline: Complexity is being recast from a theory that explains systems into an ethics of interdependence, while the co-creation workshop literature quietly hardens into training evaluation.
paras: The sharpest thing on the radar this week is Chutoranski's (2026) argument in Educational Philosophy and Theory that complexity's value no longer lies in system-theoretical explanation but in an ethical and ontological sensitivity to interdependence: forget complexity at close range so that subject-formation and response have room, remember its reach in the long chains of consequence. That is close to the substrate question you are taking to CARN, though his canon is Morin, Davis and Sumara, Haraway and Latour rather than Juarrero, Levin or Tsing. Durak et al. (2026) supply the evidence underneath it: across 357 publications, complexity science in education remains strong as theory and only partial in practice, with teachers and administrators barely studied. Dawson et al. (2026) show the other direction of travel, turning complexity leadership into a management framework for institutions absorbing generative AI.

The one lineage traced this run is instructive. Vazquez-Mendoza, Stapleton and Galvan's (2026) structured model for designing and evaluating cross-disciplinary co-creation workshops rests on Checkland's soft systems methodology (2000) by way of Jackson's critical systems practice (2006, 2025) and Midgley's community operational research (2018) - and then borrows its evaluation half from Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation (2006, 2007). Participation enters only through Scharmer (2015), Ellstrom (2020) and one review by Keahey (2021). So the model will tell you whether a workshop ran well, not whether it moved who holds the knowledge - worth knowing before you borrow it for 'Substrate Matters' or the CDC Urban Innovation sessions. Peña-del-Valle, Hare and Dinnie (2026), published 6 October in the same journal, ask the adjacent question: what researchers actually do with systems thinking once they are inside food-system work.

On design-based research the week is unusually rich. Rumiantsev et al. (2026) report four years of practitioner-led educational design research at a Dutch conservatoire, producing a shared curriculum lens, two embedded modules and transferable design principles - the nearest published template for your own work with teacher teams. Taptamat et al. (2026) run DBR through a student-staff partnership to build ethical AI literacy resources and are candid that the opt-in module barely reached anyone, which is a more useful finding than their four design principles. Choopani (2026) in EDeR treats a course itself as a knowledge-generating artefact across Germany and Iran. Alongside them, Cong-Lem and Thuy-Dung's (2026) review of 29 studies shows critical thinking being redefined around generative AI, with verification and justification as the design levers - the literature your Professional Criticality papers argue with.

On transdisciplinarity the useful item is sceptical: Rosero-Toro et al. (2026) review the distance between integrative rhetoric and actual practice, written largely from Latin America, which is exactly the counterweight the td shelf has been short of. Rosin, Lewis, Jensen et al. (2026) go the other way and name eight transdisciplinary epistemic practices grouped into exploring, meaning making and critiquing - a ready-made vocabulary for professional criticality in teaching. Chen and Mao (2026) review art-science collaboration and who actually participates in it, and Dong (2026) reads biopiracy as epistemic colonialism across India, Brazil and South Africa, which feeds the Santos strand. One practical note: the Crossref and Bluesky routes failed for the second week running, so this digest rests on Consensus, two Springer listing pages and ScienceGuide. The journal watch swept 3 of 20 journals.
